doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Tommy Flanagan years, family and Junior Mance cruises
summary: Back with Ella in 1971 with Flanagan and Thigpen, the pianist changes in Dinah's band, family support, and recent jazz cruises with Junior Mance.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: But you stuck with Tommy Flanagan for a number of years.

Well when I went with Ella, when first I went with Ella, Tommy was with her, and then when I went back in ‘71, Tommy was with her, Tom and Ed Thigpen. And Ed left in ‘72 because he had married and his wife had a baby, and they got — Bobby Durham I think it was. Yeah. And so I was Tommy, Tommy and me stayed until ‘76. Almost five years with Tommy during that period there. Yeah, ‘76 he left.
Does your family enjoy the kind of lifestyle and the kind of music you do?

Who knows? No they’ve been very supportive. I mean the kids have their own type of things, but they’ve come out to a lot of places that I was working at and — oh I was wrong, Tommy Flanagan left in ‘78 because I remember we did the Montreaux in ‘77. But that was one experience. Think of in your lifetime, just in the short amount of time you’re working with Wynton Kelly and of course Wynton had to go to the Army. I’m back tracking back to Dinah when I joined in ‘51, and then in the middle of ‘52, not quite the middle, he had to go to the Army so we got Beryl Booker down there, Beryl Booker, and she was for a while and then we had a piano player out of Chicago named Sleepy Anderson for a while, then Junior Mance went with Dinah for a while, and then when I went with Ella there was Tommy Flanagan and that puts something in your mind.
And you’ve been working with Junior Mance recently?
Yeah. On the cruise things. We did recording in New York and we were on a cruise last year and we are on again this year.
How do you like those cruises?

I love it for the point of getting away from the world you know. At least you’re out there for a week and nobody’s going to call you and say can I do this, can I do this? But they’re going to do it anyhow. No traffic, and everybody’s out there for one thing, for the music. But it’s just good to see another part of the world, which is water, which I love because I’m under the water sign, and it’s refreshing. It’s charging the batteries. And you’ll get ready to come back and as soon as you get off the ship — okay.
It all descends on you again.
Here comes all the hectic stuff, but I can handle it now.
